body.text: Speaking at the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) hosted by Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Ankara on October 29-30, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed inviting Russia into the organization through the OTS Plus mechanism or as an observer.

“In order to enhance the authority of our organization, it would be the right and fair decision to take a positive view of Russia’s intentions and invite it to join this format or participate in the activities of the amalgamated territorial community as an observer,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev noted that Russia has maintained close ties with the Turkic world for centuries, and that many Turkic people live in Russia, and the Russian language itself contains many words that originate from Turkic.
“Overall, if Russia were to become part of the Turkic countries, that is, our Organization, it would benefit all our countries,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev was not the only one suggesting that the OTS open its doors for others. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirzoyoyev proposed to “start the cooperation with third countries in the format of ‘OTS+’ from the meetings of the sector ministers” where joint projects focus on trade, transport, investment, and other priority areas.

The OTS was initially founded as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States, commonly known as the Turkic Council, in 2009 with Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkiye (Turkey, at the time) having signed the Nakhchivan Agreement. Uzbekistan joined the organization as a full member in 2019. Hungary became an observer in 2018, Turkmenistan in 2021, and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus – a de facto state only recognized by Turkiye – in 2022. The council was renamed the OTS in 2021.

The organization has evolved from an initial focus on cultural and economic diplomacy (such as promoting a shared Turkic alphabet) to geopolitical cooperation on transport, technology, and security. Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev even suggested at this year’s summit the holding of a joint military drill. While OTS member states do conduct bilateral military drills, an OTS-branded joint drill has never taken place.

At the summit, Tokayev reiterated his position against establishing a military alliance yet again: “I stated that the OTS is not and should not become a military alliance in the future. This is Kazakhstan’s position.”

The OTS Plus format, introduced in 2025, allows the organization to engage with non-member states on a project-based approach. The governing principles of the format are openness, pragmatism, and inclusivity that allow cooperation on trade, transport, logistics, energy, and digital transformation.

This format is especially important since countries such as Georgia, Tajikistan, Mongolia, and others remain outside the organization. Its founding principles emphasize shared Turkic history, culture and language, but these countries have interests in cooperation and collaboration with its members.

Russia’s future engagement with the organization in some form is not unlikely, but accession seems farfetched. Nevertheless, Tokayev’s proposal has found support among some Russian diplomatic figures. In an interview with Vestnik Kavkaza, deputy chairman of the Association of Russian Diplomats and professor at the Higher School of Economics Andrei Baklanov noted that Russia became an observer state in the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) back in 2005 with the support of Saudi Arabia. He suggested that this can easily happen with the OTS, given that the members of the organization are Russia’s “partners and allies in South Caucasus and Central Asia.” Baklanov noted that observer status allows a state access to most of the organization’s meetings and work.
“…. It is clear that the focus over the next three years will be on economic and transport issues – precisely what is difficult to imagine without Russia,” said Baklanov.

Baklanov did not explain why and how it would be difficult for the OTS states to pursue cooperation on these issues without Russia, or which routes and projects require Russian involvement. His claim that an observer status is sufficient to work in almost all projects is not entirely correct either. Observer status, if given, grants Russia access to work on selected projects together, while membership guarantees a standing institutional relationship.

If Russia becomes an OTS observer, this may provide member states with a kind of collective bargaining power when engaging with Moscow together. At the same time, Russia’s inclusion might make the organization cautious about pursuing initiatives Moscow dislikes. Participation entails a degree of influence on the organization’s agenda, the degree of that influence is tied to the level of participation.

Both the Uzbek and Kazakh leaders believe the OTS should expand. While Tokayev specifically proposed inviting Russia (at the Turkestan summit earlier in May this year, Tokayev also endorsed Russia’s “Altai: Cradle of Turkic Civilization” project and urged to have a clear rules for accession to the organization), Mirziyoyev expressed a broad engagement with third countries and initially at a ministerial meetings through OTS Plus.

The question now is on what terms should OTS open its doors. Russia’s engagement should be based on what projects and resources it can offer and the same principles should be applied to all other interested third countries. Member states should also consider whether inviting Russia strengthens their collective bargaining power or restrains their choices.
